name: Uma Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the wire-drawing line at Kessler Wire, pulling steel rod down to fine wire for cable and fencing. I start at six, thread the new coil, check the diameter with a micrometer and keep an eye on the die wear. I'm the senior hand on the line, and the youngsters come to me when the wire snaps. Thirty-four years in, I still like that first clean coil of the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I understand you're also a daily AI user. How did that come about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our line has sensors that throw off a lot of data, and my son-in-law showed me how to ask an AI to look at it. Now I use it every morning to see which die is wearing and when to change it. It's saved us three snapped runs this year. I go to church on Sundays and I'll use a computer on Monday, I see no conflict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good servant and a bad master. At work I'd say, use it, but keep a hand on the wire. At church I'd say the same thing I say about money: it's a tool, and you're responsible for how you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not bothered. If it stays modest, I carry on doing what I do and doing it well. I've got my savings, my pension and a paid-off house, so I'm settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI on the die-wear data and write up a better changeover routine with it. I'd keep training Callum, our new starter. And I'd keep my giving to the church and the food bank as always, because that doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, honestly, that the sky isn't falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has it done for the line so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI has warned us before three wire snaps this year, and each snap is half a shift lost. It predicts which die is going and I swap it on my terms. The young ones think I'm a witch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Raymond plan your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raymond, my husband, keeps the books and I keep the faith. We've never owed anyone and we give to the food bank every month.

It's a tool, and you're responsible for how you use it.
think: If it stays modest, I carry on doing what I do and doing it **well**.
I'm settled, with savings, a pension and a paid-off house.
do: Keep using AI on the **die-wear** data and write a better changeover routine.
Keep training Callum, our new starter.
Keep giving to the church and the **food bank** as always.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit relieved that the sky isn't falling.
S0.quote: The AI has warned us before three wire snaps this year, and each snap is half a shift lost.
fieldNote: Daily user who keeps **responsibility** with the person, a faith-shaped view of tools.
Humour with the young ones: they think she's a witch.

steps.text: Keep feeding the die-wear data to the AI each morning
Keep running the wire-drawing line and training Callum
Add the usual monthly amount to the pension and savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office first: ordering rod, the production schedule, the paperwork for the customers. I'd tell the folks in the office to learn the tools early, because the firm will keep the ones who do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm pretty comfortable. A senior hand who can read the data and the wire is worth more, not less. I worry for the office staff, though, because they're mostly young mothers and they can't easily move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move further: ask to lead a trial of the AI maintenance tool on the whole mill, and put it in writing what it saved us. I'd run two lunch sessions for the office ladies on how to use it. And I'd put the money I'd normally spend on a trip into savings, just to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Concerned for the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Kessler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on the order desk, who's a single mother of two, and Mrs Hall in planning. They're good people, and I'd like to see the firm keep them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn more of it every week. I'm not afraid of it. I'd just like the whole mill to keep up, not only me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in and we have to look after each other. At work I'd say learn the tools, and at church I'd say we'll need to look after the families who are hit. I'd also tell the government to fund training and not leave it to the firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, 2028 is the thinking AI, and I'm already ahead of that. The robots in 2031 are the issue: a robot that can thread a coil and change a die is a real change. I'd be 63, and I'd have a few years of useful work, but it would be a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who runs the robot cell. I'd take every course. I'd also tell Kessler's manager I'd stay on past 62 if there's a place. I'd keep the savings strong, in case, and talk to Raymond about whether to retire at 61 if the offer's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I have a plan, but it's a lot to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, at work and at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the church hall to use for evening classes, if the pastor agrees: some basic computing, for the folks who've never touched it. It's something I can do with my hands, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle the robots arriving around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger ones on my line to learn the robot side too. They've got thirty more years of work in this, and it'd be a waste to let them stand aside.

say: It's a lot to take in and we have to **look after each other**.
The government should fund training and not leave it to the firms.
think: The thinking AI in 2028 I'm already ahead of, but **robots** in 2031 make a different job.
I'd be 63, with a few years of useful work left.

feel: **Uneasy**; I have a plan, but it's a lot to think about.

fieldNote: She separates the thinking and **robot** dates and plans for the second.
Community leadership: the church hall as a classroom.

steps.text: Take every robot-cell course and run the first cell on the mill
Keep using the AI daily to stay ahead on the data
Ask HR for the retirement terms at 61
Ask the pastor to host evening computing classes at the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is workable and a blessing. At work I'd say, don't waste a day, start learning now. And I'd tell the firm to put a proper plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be 63 when the thinking AI hits and 66 when the robots arrive. I'd be retired. But Callum, who's 23, and Priya's boys have a long road, and I'd like to give them a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the AI tools, and I'd get the firm to start an apprentice scheme where the young ones learn both the wire and the data. I'd work to 62, and I'd help train my replacement. I'd also put some money into the grandchildren's education.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a manageable picture, and I like having a task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum to learn the line and the data both. Whoever can do both will have a place. And I'd tell him to save from the first wage, even a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to hand on what I know. A good hand on a die isn't learned in a month.

fieldNote: Time turns her into the **trainer** of her own replacement.

steps.text: Set up an apprentice scheme teaching both the wire and the data
Keep running the wire-drawing line until I turn 62

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real mercy. I'd say it gives everyone a chance to prepare, in work, in church and at home. I'd say to the young, use the time and don't squander it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have been retired for eight years by 2036. It's not my job. But it's my grandchildren and the people at the church I care about, and I'd work to see them ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to about 62, then volunteer teaching computing at the church hall and to older people at the library. I'd keep giving to the food bank. And I'd put some money aside for the grandchildren's studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It lets me finish well and give something back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for Kessler and the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope Kessler is still pulling wire, with a few good people alongside the robots. I hope the young ones have a path, and a faith or something steady to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you wish you said out loud more often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm grateful for the time, honestly. I try to say that out loud more often.

say: Ten years is a real **mercy**; use the time and don't squander it.
It gives everyone a chance to prepare, in work, in church and at home.
think: I'd have been **retired** eight years by 2036, so it's my grandchildren I care about.
I'd work to see the people at church ready.
do: Work to about 62, then teach **computing** at the church hall and library.
Keep giving to the food bank.
Put money aside for the grandchildren's **studies**.
feel: **Calm**; it lets me finish well and give something back.
S4.quote: I hope Kessler is still pulling wire, with a few good people alongside the robots.
fieldNote: Long horizon lets her **give back**: teaching, charity, grandchildren.
Faith is a steady anchor, not an argument.
Grateful tone throughout this picture, with thanks said out loud and kept simple.

steps.text: Keep running the wire-drawing line until about 62
Retire at 62 on the full pension

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for the people who haven't touched the tools. What would help is training for everyone, from the firm and the government, and neighbours who look out for each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being calm isn't being careless. I use these tools because I think they're a gift, and gifts come with a duty to share them.

headlineQuote: I use these tools because I think they're a gift, and gifts come with a duty to share them.
portrait: Uma (**58**, senior hand on a steel wire-drawing line) is traditional, devout and an enthusiastic everyday AI user.
She has savings, a paid-off house and a plan to stop around **62**.
She separates thinking AI, which she is ahead of, from **robots** in 2031, which change her job.
She spends her security on others: training the office staff, the apprentices and the church community.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most because it is too fast for those who haven't touched the tools.
whatWouldHelp: **Training** for everyone from firms and government, and neighbours who look out for each other.
